wine.name: Te Mata Coleraine
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, usually the larger part, with Merlot and a little Cabernet Franc; the blend moves with each vintage.
wine.sites: Chosen parcels of the estate's oldest vineyards in the Havelock Hills, on north facing slopes below Te Mata Peak, which the house tells as first planted in 1892; until 1989 Coleraine came from the single Coleraine vineyard alone.
wine.making: Each parcel is picked and fermented apart, and only the lots judged right for Coleraine are chosen for the blend. The wine is then aged in French oak barriques, new and seasoned, for around a year and a half before bottling.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackcurrant leaf and cedar over pencil shavings and a gravelly, graphite edge; medium in weight and moderate in alcohol, with fine, firm tannin and fresh acidity that keep it taut rather than ripe and broad.
wine.ageing: Closed and firm for its first eight to ten years in a strong vintage, it then opens slowly and can last for two decades and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: From the old Havelock Hills vineyards below Te Mata Peak, Te Mata Estate has blended Coleraine from Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc since the 1982 vintage. Cedar, cassis and firm, fine tannin: a red to lay down for years, then open an hour ahead.
records.story: Bernard Chambers (1859 to 1931), a sheep farmer born at Te Mata, began to plant vines on the family's land in 1892, with Pinot Noir cuttings from the Marist mission at Taradale among the first, and by the account of the national encyclopedia he had made his first wine by 1895. The house counts 1896 as its founding. By 1910 Te Mata was, on the same account, the largest wine producer in New Zealand, but prohibition campaigns, pests, frost and the loss of workers in the First World War wore it down, and in 1917 Chambers sold the winery, its stocks and part of the vineyard, and most of the station soon after. For decades the estate made little of note. In 1974 two families bought it and set about restoring the old buildings and vines. Their first Coleraine came with the 1982 vintage from the vineyard by one family's home, named for the Northern Irish town where an ancestor was born, and it stayed a single vineyard wine until 1989. In 2017 the British magazine Decanter named the 1998 Coleraine one of its Wine Legends, by the house's account the first New Zealand wine it so named. Coleraine stands as the Hawke's Bay Bordeaux blend in its classic form: restrained, cedar framed and built to age.

wine.name: Craggy Range Le Sol Syrah
wine.sites: The house's Gimblett Gravels vineyard west of Hastings, bought and first planted in 1998, on greywacke stones with layers of silt and sand, inland and sheltered from the cooling sea breeze.
wine.making: The blocks are fermented apart, in recent years in French oak vats and open stainless steel fermenters, often with native yeast and a share of whole bunches that runs from none to about two thirds by vintage, with three to four weeks on the skins. The wine is then raised for around a year and a half in French oak barriques with Austrian oak barriques, demi-muids or puncheons, a minority new.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and violet over black pepper and graphite, with a smoky, savoury edge; medium to full bodied, with fine grained tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Open enough to enjoy within a few years of release, it gains savoury depth over a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large Syrah or Burgundy glass.

records.table: Le Sol Syrah grows on the old Ngaruroro riverbed, in Craggy Range's own Gimblett Gravels vineyard, and was first made in 2001. Blackberry, violet and black pepper over fine tannin: cool climate Syrah, nearer the northern Rhône than the Barossa.
records.story: A stony block on the Gimblett Gravels, the old bed of the Ngaruroro River west of Hastings, was bought and first planted in 1998, the year an Australian family founded Craggy Range with a Master of Wine as its partner in the venture, by the house's own account; a vineyard at Te Muna Road in Martinborough followed for Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc, and the cellar door was built near Havelock North. The first commercial vintage was 2001, and with it came the three reds the house built its name on: Le Sol from Syrah, Sophia from Merlot and The Quarry from Cabernet Sauvignon. In the same year, 2001, the growers of the Gimblett Gravels formed their own association and defined their district by its soil rather than by a line on a map, a step the association believes was a first for the New World. On those stones Le Sol gives Syrah peppered and perfumed, fresher than its warm Australian cousins.

wine.sites: The house's Mere Road vineyard on the Gimblett Gravels, west of Hastings, where a thin skin of sandy loam lies over the old river gravel.
wine.making: The grapes are partly crushed and fermented warm in small batches. The wine is then aged for about a year in French oak barrels, a quarter to a third of them new, before it is blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black cherry and black pepper with mocha and roasted chestnut from the oak, and a flinty, smoky edge; rich and concentrated, with ripe, fine tannin.

records.table: Marist missionaries began Mission Estate Winery with vines planted in 1851, and it is told as New Zealand's oldest surviving winery. From the Mere Road vineyard on the Gimblett Gravels, its Jewelstone Syrah gives blackberry, pepper and mocha, rich and supple.
records.story: The Catholic Marist mission came to Hawke's Bay from the north and planted its first vines at Pakowhai in 1851, chiefly to make wine for the Mass and the table; the winery counts that year as its founding, and the national encyclopedia names it the country's oldest surviving winemaker. In 1858 the mission moved to Meeanee, where it built a seminary and kept its vines for half a century, and in 1871, by the house's account, a French brother arrived there and extended the vineyards; its Huchet range carries his name. Floods on the plain drove the mission to higher ground at Greenmeadows in Taradale: in late 1910, as the house tells it, its main house was cut into eleven sections and hauled nearly five kilometres by traction engine, and the seminary moved there in 1911. Syrah from the Gimblett Gravels later became one of its strengths. Jewelstone is the small batch tier the house sets just below Huchet, and its Syrah puts a glass of the country's earliest wine history on the table.

wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand and fermented in small open vats, plunged by hand, with some parcels left as whole bunches and some, in some years, fermented with Viognier skins. wine.glass: Blackberry, black plum and violet over cracked pepper, smoked meat and a floral lift; dense yet fresh, with firm, fine grained tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first five to eight years, it is made for the long term, and the house says a strong vintage can be kept for twenty years.

records.table: Cuttings from the hill of Hermitage gave the vines behind Trinity Hill's Homage Syrah, made on the Gimblett Gravels since 2002 and only in strong years. Blackberry, violet and pepper, dense and firm, it wants a decanter: the region's answer to the northern Rhône.
records.story: On a barren plot of the old Ngaruroro riverbed off Gimblett Road, Trinity Hill's partners planted their first vines in 1993, the year the house was founded, among the early growers on what came to be called the Gimblett Gravels. Its first commercial vintage came in 1996. Later that year the founding winemaker worked the harvest at Paul Jaboulet Aîné in Hermitage, and the Jaboulet family gave him Syrah cuttings from the hill of Hermitage, and Viognier from Côte-Rôtie came with them, as the house tells it. The vines passed through quarantine and were propagated and planted on the estate, and Homage, first made with the 2002 vintage, was named in tribute to the Rhône house and the family member who gave them. It is made only in years the house judges strong enough, in small amounts, and was soon one of the wines that drew attention to Gimblett Gravels Syrah abroad. Homage carries the Rhône roots of Hawke's Bay Syrah in one bottle: vines from Hermitage, fermented in the northern manner, grown on New Zealand river stones.

wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, the balance moving with each vintage; the early releases were mostly Cabernet, and Merlot has weighed more since 1998.
wine.sites: The house's Redstone vineyard in the Bridge Pa Triangle and its vineyards on the Gimblett Gravels, both on warm, free draining soils of the old river plain.
wine.making: The parcels are fermented apart, the Cabernet Sauvignon in some years in large French oak vats and the Merlot in stainless steel. The wine then finishes its malolactic and is aged in French oak barriques, a large share new, for fifteen months to over two years by vintage, and it is made only in years the house judges exceptional.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, plum and cedar with cocoa and toasted, nutty oak; full and fleshy, with supple yet firm tannin and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and oaky in youth, it wants eight to ten years in a strong vintage and can last for two decades or more.

records.table: Named for Tom McDonald, who made the cellar's name, TOM is Church Road's Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, first made in 1995 and only in exceptional years. Blackcurrant, cedar and firm, supple tannin; it repays a long wait in the cellar.
records.story: A settler from Luxembourg founded the winery on Church Road in Taradale in 1897, on land beside the Marist mission. Tom McDonald (1907 to 1987), born at Greenmeadows, started in its cellar in 1921 and, by his own account, bought the business in 1927, aged nineteen. In 1944 he sold it to Ballins Breweries and stayed on to run it; a new winery went up on Church Road in 1948, and in 1949 he made a Cabernet Sauvignon that is told as one of New Zealand's first commercial wines of the grape. In 1962 the firm, by then McDonald's Wines, merged with McWilliam's, and he became its production director. Montana bought the Taradale winery in the late 1980s, renovated it and named it Church Road, and the cellar passed with Montana to Allied Domecq in 2001 and with Allied Domecq to Pernod Ricard in 2005. TOM came from the 1995 vintage and was unveiled in 1999 with the opening of a cellar named for McDonald. It is made only in years the house judges exceptional, a modern Hawke's Bay Cabernet blend that keeps the name of the man behind the Cabernet of 1949.

questions.exp: TOM blends fruit from the house's Redstone vineyard in the Bridge Pa Triangle and its Gimblett Gravels vineyards; the Havelock Hills are Te Mata's home, not Church Road's.

questions.q: In which year, by his own account, did Tom McDonald, aged nineteen, buy the winery that became Church Road?
questions.exp: McDonald bought the business in 1927; 1897 is its founding, 1949 his first Cabernet Sauvignon and 1962 the merger with McWilliam's, after he had sold to Ballins Breweries in 1944.

report: The founder, Bartholomew Steinmetz, is described rather than named: his dates were not found. His being born in Luxembourg and his land coming from the Marist brothers rest on two merchant and press accounts.
Montana's purchase is 1988 in two accounts and 1989 in Te Ara, so the story says the late 1980s. The 1936 purchase year in one account is set aside for Te Ara's 1927.
The 1949 Cabernet Sauvignon as one of the country's first commercial wines of the grape is told as told, from Te Ara and the press; the record does not call it the first.

Fermenting the Cabernet in French oak vats and the Merlot in steel rests on one vintage note (2007) and is hedged as some years; barrel time runs 18 to 27 months across the notes read, so around a year and a half.
Whether Pernod Ricard still holds the winery is not told, being volatile; ownership is told to 2005 only.

changed: story: the founder's going back to Europe and McDonald's lease were in no source read (one account has the founder dying in 1936); now McDonald started in the cellar in 1921 and bought the business in 1927 by his own account (Te Ara).
story: the sale to Ballins Breweries in 1944, with McDonald staying on, added (Te Ara); the new winery of 1948 is no longer told as his own building.
story: the merger of 1962 now says the firm was by then McDonald's Wines and he became production director (Te Ara and a winery history).
wine.grapes and wine.label: Cabernet usually the larger part refuted (the 2007 was 51 to 49, and Merlot has weighed more since 1998); the label no longer says the larger share is named first.
wine.making: the barrel time runs 15 to 27 months across the notes, so fifteen months to over two years, not around a year and a half; the malolactic in barrel added.

others: the McDonald Series launch year of 2012 was in no source read and is cut; Church Road 1 is told as one of the prestige wines beside TOM; the TOM Syrah's first vintage of 2013 added (the Listener).
questions[1]: the purchase of 1927 is asked as McDonald's own account.
open: Montana's purchase is 1988 in two accounts and 1989 in Te Ara: kept as the late 1980s.
